                                            The Galois Alperin weight conjecture for finite category algebras
                                                                                    Xin Huang




                                          Abstract
                                          Let p be a prime, k an algebraic closure of Fp and Γ the Galois group Gal(k/Fp ). Let C be a




arXiv:2604.06166v3 [math.RT] 7 May 2026
                                          finite category and OC the p-orbit category of C defined by Linckelmann [4]. We formulate a
                                          version of the Galois Alperin weight conjecture (GAWC) for finite category algebras stating
                                          that there exists a Γ × Aut(C)-equivariant bijection between the set of isomorphism classes
                                          of simple kC-modules and that of the weights of kOC . We reduce the GAWC for finite
                                          categories to finite groups. For C an EI-category, we give a partition of weights of kOC with
                                          respect to blocks of kC and then formulate a blockwise Galois Alperin weight conjecture
                                          (BGAWC) for C. Similarly, we reduce the BGAWC for finite EI-categories to finite groups.
                                          Keywords: Alperin’s weight conjecture, Galois automorphisms, category algebras, blocks,
                                          reduction theorems


                                          1. Introduction
                                              The (blockwise) Galois Alperin weight conjecture, due to Navarro [7], a strong form
                                          of Alperin’s weight conjecture [1], predicts that the fields of values of irreducible Brauer
                                          characters (of a block) of a finite group can be locally determined. In this paper we extend
                                          the (blockwise) Galois Alperin weight conjecture from finite groups to finite categories.
                                              Throughout this paper we fix a prime number p and an algebraic closure k of Fp and
                                          denote by Γ the Galois group Gal(k/Fp ). A category C is called finite if its morphism class
                                          is a finite set. Any finite group can be viewed as a finite category with one object.
                                              Let C be a finite category. According to [4, Definition 1.1], the p-transporter category of C
                                          is the finite category TC defined as follows. The objects of TC are the pairs (X, P ) consisting
                                          of an object X of C and a not necessarily unitary p-subgroup P of the monoid EndC (X).
                                          For any two objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q), the morphism set HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is the set
                                          of all triples (s, P, Q) where s : X → Y is a morphism in C satisfying s = s ◦ 1P = 1Q ◦ s and
                                          s ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s. The composition of morphisms in TC is induced by that in C. The identity
                                          morphism of an object (X, P ) in TC is (1P , P, P ). If no confusion arise, we will denote
                                          a morphism (s, P, Q) in TC again by s. Allowing nonunitary subgroups P of EndC (X) in
                                          the definition of objects of TC means that the unit element 1P of P need not be equal
                                          to IdX but can be any idempotent endomorphism of X. The condition s = s ◦ 1P =
                                          1Q ◦ s in this definition implies that HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) can be identified to a subset of
                                          1Q ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ 1P . With this identification, the morphism set HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is a
                                          Q-P -subbiset of 1Q ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ 1P with respect to the actions induced by precomposing
                                          with morphisms in P and composing with morphisms in Q. The condition s ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s in
                                                                                         1
the above implies that Q ◦ s ◦ P = Q ◦ s; that is, any Q-P -orbit in HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q))
is in fact a Q-orbit. According to [4, Definition 1.2], the p-orbit category of C is the finite
category OC defined as follows. The objects of OC are the same as those of TC . For any two
objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q) of OC , the morphism set HomOC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is the set of all
Q-P -orbits Q\HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q))/P of morphisms in TC . The composition of morphisms
in OC is induced by that in TC .
    For a finite-dimensional k-algebra A, denote by S(A) the set of isomorphism classes of
simple A-modules. Following [6], given a finite category C, the isomorphism classes of simple
kC-modules are parametrised by isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ), with e an idempotent
endomorphism of some object X in C and T a simple kGe -module, where Ge is the group of
all invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e. Such a pair (e, T ) is called a weight
of kC if the simple kGe -module T is in addition projective. Denote by W(kC) the set of
isomorphism classes of weights of kC; we review this in Section 3 below. The group-theoretic
version of Alperin’s weight conjecture in [1] is equivalent to the following statement:

Conjecture 1.1 (Alperin [1]). For any finite group G, there exists a bijection between S(kG)
and W(kOG ).

   Linckelmann [4] extended Conjecture 1.1 to finite categories:

Conjecture 1.2 (Linckelmann [4, Conjecture 1.3]). For any finite category C, there exists
a bijection between S(kC) and W(kOC ).

    In [4, Corollary 1.5], Linckelmann showed that Conjectures 1.2 and 1.1 are in fact equiv-
alent. To consider the action of the Galois group Γ, we need the following notation:

Notation 1.3. Let A be a finite-dimensional Fp -algebra and let A′ := k ⊗Fp A. Let σ ∈ Γ.
We see that σ induces an Fp -algebra automorphism of A′ sending x ⊗ a to σ(x) ⊗ a for
any x ∈ k and a ∈ A. We abusively use the same symbol σ to denote this Fp -algebra
automorphism. Clearly Γ permutes the set of (primitive) central idempotents of A′ . For any
A′ -module U , denote by σ U the A′ -module which is equal to U as a k-module endowed with
                                    σ −1
the structure homomorphism A′ −−→ A′ → Endk (U ). Sometimes we will also write σ U as
                                         ′                                                ′
σ U . Note that if f : U → V is an A -module homomorphism, then f is also an A -module
homomorphism σ U → σ V . One checks that the map sending x ⊗ a to σ −1 (x) ⊗ a induces
an isomorphism of A′ -modules A′ ∼    = σ A′ , where x ∈ k ′ and a ∈ A. Now it is clear that σ U
is a simple (resp. projective) A′ -module if and only if U is simple (resp. projective). Hence
the group Γ acts on the set S(A′ ). Moreover, if b is a central idempotent of A′ , then Γb (the
stabiliser of b in Γ) acts on the set S(A′ b). By Proposition 2.5 below, if C is a finite category
and α ∈ Z 2 (C; F× p ), then Γ also acts on the set of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kα C.

   In [7], Navarro predicted a Galois refinement of the Alperin weight conjecture for finite
group which can be reformulated as follows:

Conjecture 1.4 (Navarro [7]; cf. [11, Conjecture]). For any finite group G, there exists a
bijection S(kG) → W(kOG ) commuting with the action of Γ.
                                                2
   This leads to the obvious extension to finite categories:

Conjecture 1.5. For any finite category C, there exists a bijection S(kC) → W(kOC )
commuting with the action of Γ.

    If we forget the action of Γ, then Conjecture 1.5 returns to Linckelmann’s Conjecture 1.2.
Similar to Linckelmann’s result [4, Theorem 1.4], we show that Conjectures 1.4 and 1.5 are in
fact equivalent. This equivalence holds more generally for twisted group algebras and twisted
category algebras with a 2-cocycle in Z 2 (C; F×   p ) which is extendible to the orbit category.
There are canonical functors from C to TC and OC sending an object X in C to (X, {IdX }),
and a morphism in C to its obvious images in TC and OC , respectively. In particular, every
                                                                  ×
2-cocycle α in Z 2 (OC ; F×                                 2
                          p ) restricts to a 2-cocycle in Z (C; Fp ), again denoted by α.

Theorem 1.6. Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; F×   p ). If for any idempotent
endomorphism e in C, there is a Γ-equivariant bijection S(kα Ge ) → W(kα OGe ), then there
exists a Γ-equivariant bijection S(kα C) → W(kα OC ).

   This will be proved in Section 3.

Corollary 1.7. Conjectures 1.4 and 1.5 are equivalent.

Remark 1.8. (i) In Theorem 1.6, the reason why we require α to be a 2-cocycle with
coefficients in F×                                   ∼
                 p is that in this case we have kα C = k ⊗Fp (Fp )α C, and then the Galois group
Γ has an action on S(kα C) as described in Notation 1.3.
   (ii) Note that the formulation in Theorem 1.6 for twisted category algebras requires
the 2-cocycle α to be the restriction to C of a 2-cocycle of OC along the canonical functor
                                                                     ×
C → OC . It is not clear whether the map H 2 (OC ; F×         2
                                                      p ) → H (C; Fp ) induced by the canonical
functor C → OC is injective or surjective in general. The corresponding canonical functor
C → TC sending X to (X, {IdX }) poses no problem:

Proposition 1.9 (cf. [4, Proposition 1.6]). Let C be a finite category. The canonical functor
C → TC induces a graded isomorphism H ∗ (TC ; F×    ∼ ∗        ×
                                                p ) = H (C; Fp ).

    As Linckelmann mentioned in [4], it is less clear what happens under the functor TC → OC
in general. We have the following special case for EI-categories (i.e. categories in which all
endomorphisms are isomorphisms):

Proposition 1.10 (cf. [4, Proposition 1.7]). Let C be a finite EI-category. Then TC and
OC are EI-categories, and the canonical functor C → OC induces a graded isomorphism
H ∗ (OC ; F×   ∼ ∗      ×
           p ) = H (C; Fp ).

    One checks that the proofs of [4, Propositions 1.6, 1.7, 4.6] did not use the blanket
assumption there that the ground field is algebraically closed - we can replace the coefficient
field there by any perfect field of characteristic p.



                                               3
Example 1.11. Brauer algebras, Temperley–Lieb algebras, partition algebras, and their
cyclotomic analogues can be interpreted as twisted monoid algebras (cf. [12]). The 2-cocycles
of the underlying monoids for these algebras satisfy the hypotheses of [4, Proposition 4.6];
in particular, they are constant on maximal subgroups (so that their restrictions to maximal
subgroups represent the trivial classes) and they extend to the associated orbit categories.
Using a recent result in [2] that the BGAWC holds for symmetric groups, it is easy to see
that the maximal subgroups of the underlying diagram monoids satisfy the GAWC, and
hence so do these diagram algebras.

    Since there is a blockwise Galois Alperin weight conjecture (BGAWC) for finite group,
one will ask whether there is a BGAWC for a finite category C. For this question we need
to first give a partition of the weights of the orbit category algebra kOC with respect to
blocks of kC. Unfortunately, for the general case we didn’t find such a partition. But if C
is an EI-category, we can give such a partition; see Definition 5.4 below. For any central
idempotent b of a finite EI-category C, we define the notion of a b-weight of kOC . If b = 1,
then W(kOC , b) returns to W(kOC ). We can easily show that Γb acts on W(kOC , b); see
Definition 5.4.
    A finite group can be regarded as a finite EI-category, and the BGAWC for finite groups
can be reformulated as follows:

Conjecture 1.12 (Navarro [7]; cf. [3, Conjecture 2]). For any finite group G and any
central idempotent b of kG, there exists a bijection S(kGb) → W(kOG , b) commuting with
the action of Γb .

   This leads to the obvious extension to finite EI-categories:

Conjecture 1.13. For any finite EI-category C and any central idempotent b of kC, there
exists a bijection S(kCb) → W(kOC , b) commuting with the action of Γb .

   If we take b = 1, then Conjecture 1.13 returns to Conjecture 1.5. We show that Conjec-
tures 1.12 and 1.13 are in fact equivalent. As in the block-free case, this equivalence holds
more generally for twisted group algebras and twisted category algebras:

Theorem 1.14. Let C be a finite EI-category, b a central idempotent of kC, and α ∈
Z 2 (OC ; F×                                                                          −1
           p ). Then for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, setting ê = α(e, e) e, êb
is a central idempotent in kα Ge ; see Proposition 5.1 below. If for any idempotent endomor-
phism e in C, there is a Γb -equivariant bijection S(kα Ge êb) → W(kα OGe , êb), then there
exists a Γb -equivariant bijection S(kα Cb) → W(kα OC , b).

   This will be proved in Section 5 after we investigate the Brauer construction on twisted
group algebras in Section 4.

Corollary 1.15. Conjectures 1.12 and 1.13 are equivalent.

    Let C be finite category. Recall that a functor F : C → C is called an automorphism
of C if there is another functor G : C → C such that F ◦ G = IdC = G ◦ F. Let Aut(C)
                                             4
denote the group of automorphisms of the category C. Clearly if C is a finite group G, then
Aut(C) = Aut(G). We can formulate analogues of Conjectures 1.2 and 1.13 with Aut(C)
instead of Γ. We need the following notation:

Notation 1.16. Let F be an automorphism of a finite category C. Then for any objects
X and Y in C, F induces an isomorphism FX,Y : HomC (X, Y ) ∼  = HomC (F(X), F(Y )); for
shorthand we abusively denote the isomorphism FX,Y by F. As X and Y run over all
objects in C, those isomorphisms FX,Y induce a k-algebra automorphism of kC sending any
s ∈ HomC (X, Y ) to F(s); we still use the symbol F to denote this automorphism of kC.
Clearly F permutes the set of (primitive) central idempotents of kC. For any kC-module
U , denote by F U the kC-module which is equal to U as a k-module endowed with the
                              F −1
structure homomorphism kC −−→ kC → Endk (U ). Note that if f : U → V is an kC-module
homomorphism, then f is also a kC-module homomorphism F U → F V . One checks that the
map sending a to F −1 (a) induces an isomorphism of kC-modules kC ∼    = F kC, where a ∈ kC.
Now it is clear that F U is a simple (resp. projective) kC-module if and only if U is simple
(resp. projective). Hence the group Aut(C) acts on the set S(kC). Moreover, if b is a central
idempotent of kC, then Aut(C)b (the stabiliser of b in Aut(C)b ) acts on the set S(kCb). By
6.5 (i) below, Aut(C) also acts on the set of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kOC . If C is
an EI-category, then Aut(C)b acts on W(kOC , b); see 6.5 (ii).

    The following conjecture is extracted from the inductive (blockwise) Alperin weight con-
dition:

Conjecture 1.17 (Navarro–Tiep [8, 3.2]; Späth [9, Definition 4.2 (ii)]). (i) For any finite
      group G, there exists a bijection S(kG) → W(kOG ) commuting with the action of
      Aut(G).
 (ii) For any finite group G and any central idempotent b of kG, there exists a bijection
      S(kGb) → W(kOG , b) commuting with the action of Aut(G)b .

   This leads to the following extension to finite categories:

Conjecture 1.18. (i) For any finite category C, there exists a bijection S(kC) → W(kOC )
      commuting with the action of Aut(C).
 (ii) For any finite EI-category C and any central idempotent b of kC, there exists a bijection
      S(kCb) → W(kOC , b) commuting with the action of Aut(C)b .

   Combining Conjectures 1.18 and 1.13, there is an even stronger conjecture:

Conjecture 1.19. Let C be a finite category (resp. EI-category) and b the unit element
(resp. a central idempotent) of kC. Then there exists a bijection S(kCb) → W(kOC , b)
commuting with the action of (Γ × Aut(C))b , the stabiliser of b in Γ × Aut(C).

   As before, we reduce Conjectures 1.18 and 1.19 to finite groups:



                                              5
Theorem 1.20. Let C be a finite category (resp. EI-category) and b the unit element (resp.
a central idempotent) of kC. Then for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, eb is a cen-
tral idempotent in kGe ; see Proposition 5.1. Let H be any subgroup of Γb . Assume that
for any idempotent endomorphism e in C there is an (H × Aut(Ge ))be -equivariant bijec-
tion S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb). Then there exists an (H × Aut(C))b -equivariant bijection
S(kCb) → W(kOC , b).
   This will be proved in Section 6.
Corollary 1.21. If Conjecture 1.19 holds for all finite groups, then it holds for all finite
categories. In particular, Conjectures 1.17 and 1.18 are equivalent.

2. Twisted category algebras and their idempotent endomorphisms
   Let R be a commutative ring. For two R-algebras A and B, an R-algebra isomorphism
φ : A → B and an A-module U , we denote by φ U the B-module which is equal to U as
                                                                   φ−1
an R-module endowed with the structure homomorphism B −−→ A → EndR (U ). Unless
otherwise specified, all modules (actions) in this paper are left modules (actions). Let C be
a finite category. The set of idempotent endomorphisms of objects in C is partially ordered,
with partial order given by e ≤ f whenever e and f are idempotents endomorphisms of an
object X in C satisfying e = e ◦ f = f ◦ e. Two idempotent endomorphisms e and f of
objects X and Y , respectively, are called isomorphic if there are morphisms s : X → Y and
t : Y → X satisfying t ◦ s = e and s ◦ t = f . In this case, s and t can be chosen such
that s = f ◦ s = s ◦ e and t = e ◦ t = t ◦ f ; indeed, using that e and f are idemptents, we
have e = t ◦ s = e ◦ t ◦ s ◦ t ◦ s ◦ e = (e ◦ t ◦ f ) ◦ (f ◦ s ◦ e), and a similar argument yields
f = (f ◦ s ◦ e) ◦ (e ◦ s ◦ f ). Let α be a 2-cocycle in Z 2 (C; R× ); that is, α is a map sending
any two morphisms s and t in Mor(C) for which t ◦ s is defined to a element α(t, s) in R× ,
such that for any three morphisms s, t and u for which the compositions t ◦ s and u ◦ t
are defined, we have the 2-cocycle identity α(u, t ◦ s)α(t, s) = α(u ◦ t, s)α(u, t). The twisted
category algebra Rα C is the free R-module having the morphism set Mor(C) as an R-basis,
with an R-bilinear multiplication given by ts = α(t, s)t ◦ s if t ◦ s is defined, and ts = 0
otherwise. The 2-cocycle identity is equivalent to the associativity of this multiplication.
The isomorphism class of Rα C depends only on the class of α in H 2 (C; R× ); see e.g. [5,
Theorem 1.4.7 (iii)]. So if α represents the trivial class in H 2 (C; R× ) then Rα C ∼  = RC, the
usual category algebra of C over R. For any idempotent endomorphism e of an object X in C,
we denote by Ge the group of all invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e; following
Linckelmann [4], we call such a group Ge a maximal subgroup of C. The restriction of α to
the group Ge is abusively again denoted by α. Note that the image in Rα C of an idempotent
endomorphism e of an object in C is not necessarily an idempotent; more precisely, e2 in
Rα C is equal to α(e, e)e, and hence ê = α(e, e)−1 e is an idempotent in Rα C. However, we
have êRα Cê = eRα Ce. Note that if C is an EI-category, then for any object X in C, IdX is
the unique idempotent in EndC (X) and we have GIdX = EndC (X).
Proposition 2.1. Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ). The unit element of
Rα C is X∈Ob(C) α(IdX , IdX )−1 IdX .

Proposition 2.2 ([6, Propositions 5.2, 5.4]). Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ).
If e and f are isomorphic idempotents in C, then there is an R-algebra isomorphism φ :
Rα Ge ∼ = Rα Gf , which is uniquely determined up to an inner automorphism. More explic-
itly, the following hold:
  (i) Assume that e and f are idempotent endomorphisms of objects X and Y , respectively,
      in C. Assume that s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t ◦ s = e
      and s ◦ t = f . For x ∈ Ge , set β(x) = α(x, t)α(s, x ◦ t)α(e, e)−1 α(t, s)−1 . Then the map
      φ sending x ∈ Ge to β(x)(s ◦ x ◦ t) induces an R-algebra isomorphism Rα Ge ∼         = Rα Gf .
 (ii) Assume that s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t′ ◦ s′ = e
                      ′                             ′

      and s′ ◦ t′ = f . For any y ∈ Gf , set β ′ (y) = α(y, s′ )α(t′ , y ◦ s′ )α(f, f )−1 α(s′ , t′ )−1 .
      Then the map sending x ∈ Ge to β(x)β ′ (s ◦ x ◦ t)(t′ ◦ s ◦ x ◦ t ◦ s′ ) induces an inner
      automorphism of the R-algebra Rα Ge ; it coincides with conjugation by t′ ◦ s in kα Ge .
Definition 2.3. Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ). Let e be an idempotent
endomorphism in C. For any Rα C-module U , the R-space eU = êU is an eRα Ce-module (or
equivalently, an êRα Cê-module), hence restricts to an Rα Ge -module. Two pairs (e, U ) and
(f, V ), consisting of idempotents e ∈ EndC (X), f ∈ EndC (Y ), an Rα Ge -module U and an
Rα Gf module V , are called isomorphic if the idempotents e and f are isomorphic and if the
isomorphism classes of U and V correspond to each other through the induced isomorphism
φ : Rα Ge ∼ = Rα Gf in Proposition 2.2 (i). That is, φ U ∼
                                                         = V as Rα Gf -modules. Since inner
automorphisms of an R-algebra stabilise all isomorphism classes of modules, by Proposition
2.2 (ii) this property is independent of the choice of the isomorphism φ : Rα Ge ∼
                                                                                 = Rα Gf .
Theorem 2.4 ([6, Theorem 1.2]). Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ). The map
sending a simple Rα C-module S to the pair (e, eS), where e is an idempotent endomorphism
in C minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0, induces a bijection Π between S(Rα C) and the set of
isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a
simple Rα Ge -module T .
Proposition 2.5. Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; F×         2     ×
                                                                    p ) ⊆ Z (C; k ). There is
a well-defined action of the Galois group Γ = Gal(k/Fp ) on the set of isomorphism classes
of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a simple kα Ge -module
T via σ (e, T ) = (e, σ T ), where σ ∈ Γ. Sometimes we will also write σ (e, T ) as σ (e, T ).
Moreover, (e, T ) is a weight if and only if (e, σ T ) is a weight.

Proposition 2.6. Keep the notation of Theorem 2.4. Assume that R = k and α ∈
Z 2 (C; F×
         p ). Then the bijection Π commutes with the action of the Galois group Γ.

Proof. Let σ ∈ Γ and S a simple kα C-module. Denote by [S] the isomorphism class of S.
Let e be an idempotent endomorphism in C, minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0. Then σ S is
a simple kα C-module, e(σ S) is a kα Ge -module, and e(σ S) ∼   = σ (eS) as kα Ge -modules. Hence
by the minimality of e, we see that e is also minimal with respect to e(σ S) ̸= 0. Therefore,
we have
               Π([σ S]) = [(e, e(σ S))] = [(e, σ (eS))] = σ [(e, eS)] = σ (Π([S])),
where the notation [(e, S)] denotes the isomorphism class of (e, S), and where the third
equality holds by Proposition 2.5.
Notation 2.7. Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (C; k × ). For any two isomorphic
idempotents e and f in C, we denote by Λe,f : S(kα Ge ) → S(kα Gf ) the bijection sending
[T ] ∈ S(kα Ge ) to [φ T ], where φ is the isomorphism kα Ge ∼
                                                             = kα Gf as described in Proposition
2.2 (i). Since inner automorphisms of a k-algebra stabilise all isomorphism classes of modules,
Λe,f is independent of the choice of φ. It is clear that the inverse of Λe,f is Λf,e . Moreover,
one easily checks that for any three isomorphic idempotents d, e and f in C, we have
Λe,f ◦ Λd,e = Λd,f . If α ∈ Z 2 (C; F× p ), then Λe,f commutes with the action of Γ. Indeed, by
the explicit construction of the isomorphism φ in Proposition 2.2 (i), φ is defined over Fp .
For any σ ∈ Γ, by the proof of Proposition 2.5, we have σ (φ T ) ∼ = φ (σ T ) as kα Gf -modules.
                                                    8
Proposition 2.8. Let C be a finite category. Let (X, P ) and (Y, Q) be objects in TC . Let
(e, P, P ) and (f, Q, Q) be idempotent endomorphisms of (X, P ) and (Y, Q), respectively. The
following are equivalent:
  (i) The morphisms (e, P, P ) and (f, Q, Q) are isomorphic in TC .
 (ii) There exist s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t ◦ s = e,
      s ◦ t = f and s ◦ (e ◦ P ) ◦ t = f ◦ Q.

Proof. Since (e, P, P ) and (f, Q, Q) are respectively endomorphisms of (X, P ) and (Y, Q),
we have

     e = e ◦ 1P = 1P ◦ e,    e ◦ P ⊆ P ◦ e,      f = f ◦ 1Q = 1Q ◦ f         and f ◦ Q ⊆ Q ◦ f.

From the inclusion e ◦ P ⊆ P ◦ e we see that e ◦ P = e ◦ P ◦ e is a p-subgroup of Ge . Similarly,
f ◦ Q = f ◦ Q ◦ f is a p-subgroup of Gf .
    Suppose (i) holds. By definition of being isomorphic, there exist morphisms s′ ∈ HomC (X, Y )
and t′ ∈ HomC (Y, X) such that

           s′ = s′ ◦ 1P = 1Q ◦ s′ ,    t′ = t′ ◦ 1Q = 1P ◦ t′ ,     t′ ◦ s′ = e,   s′ ◦ t′ = f

                             s′ ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s′     and t′ ◦ Q ⊆ P ◦ t′ .
Set s = f ◦s′ ◦e and t = e◦t′ ◦f . Then we have t◦s = e and s◦t = f . Consider the inclusion
s′ ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s′ . Composing with f and precomposing with e yields f ◦ s′ ◦ P ◦ e ⊆ f ◦ Q ◦ s′ ◦ e.
Using e ◦ P ◦ e = e ◦ P ⊆ P ◦ e and f ◦ Q = f ◦ Q ◦ f , we obtain (f ◦ s′ ◦ e) ◦ (e ◦ P ) ⊆
(f ◦ Q) ◦ (f ◦ s′ ◦ e), or equivalently,

                                      s ◦ (e ◦ P ) ⊆ (f ◦ Q) ◦ s.

A similarly argument applied to the inclusion t′ ◦ Q ⊆ P ◦ t′ shows that

                                      t ◦ (f ◦ Q) ⊆ (e ◦ P ) ◦ t.

Using that t ◦ s = e and s ◦ t = f , we easily see that the two inclusions above should be
equalities. Thus (i) implies (ii).
    Now suppose (ii) holds. Consider the objects (X, e◦P ) and (Y, f ◦Q) in TC . The equalities
e◦P = e◦P ◦e and f ◦Q = f ◦Q◦f implies that (e, e◦P, e◦P ) is an idempotent endomorphism
of (X, e◦P ) and (f, f ◦Q, f ◦Q) is an idempotent endomorphism of (Y, f ◦Q). By assumption,
we see that s and t define morphisms (s, e◦P, f ◦Q) : (X, e◦P ) → (Y, f ◦Q) and (t, f ◦Q, e◦P ) :
(Y, f ◦Q) → (X, e◦P ) in TC . Moreover, we have (t, f ◦Q, e◦P )◦(s, e◦P, f ◦Q) = (e, e◦P, e◦P )
and (s, e◦P, f ◦Q)◦(t, f ◦Q, e◦P ) = (f, f ◦Q, f ◦Q). Hence (e, e◦P, e◦P ) and (f, f ◦Q, f ◦Q)
are isomorphic idempotents in TC . Then by [4, Lemma 3.1 (iv)], (e, P, P ) and (f, Q, Q) are
isomorphic in TC . This shows that (i) is a consequence of (ii).

Proposition 2.9. Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; F×  p ). Let (X, P ) and (Y, Q) be
objects in TC . Assume that (e, P, P ) and (f, Q, Q) are isomorphic idempotent endomorphisms
                                                   9
in TC , or equivalently, there exist s ∈ f ◦HomC (X, Y )◦e and t ∈ e◦HomC (Y, X)◦f satisfying
t ◦ s = e, s ◦ t = f and s ◦ (e ◦ P ) ◦ t = f ◦ Q. The k-algebra isomorphism φ : kα Ge ∼    =
kα Gf described in Proposition 2.2 restricts to a k-algebra isomorphism kα NGe (e ◦ P ) ∼   =
kα NGf (f ◦ Q), which in turn induces a k-algebra isomorphism φ̄ : kα NGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) ∼
                                                                                            =
kα NGf (f ◦ Q)/(f ◦ Q).

Proof. The map sending x ∈ Ge to s ◦ x ◦ t is a group isomorphism Ge ∼       = Gf and it restricts
to group isomorphisms e ◦ P ∼       =  f ◦ Q and N Ge (e ◦ P ) ∼ N
                                                               = Gf   (f ◦ Q). Hence it induces a
                                             ∼
group isomorphism NGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) = NGf (f ◦ Q)/(f ◦ Q). By the explicit construction
of the isomorphism φ, we see that φ restricts to a k-linear isomorphism kα NGe (e ◦ P ) ∼         =
kα NGf (f ◦ Q). This is also a k-algebra isomorphism because φ respects multiplication. Since
α is taken from Z 2 (OC ; F×  p ), for any x, y ∈ NGe (e ◦ P ), α(x, y) = 1 if one of x or y is in
e ◦ P . Similarly, for any x′ , y ′ ∈ NGf (f ◦ Q), α(x′ , y ′ ) = 1 if one of x′ or y ′ is in f ◦ Q.
Hence the isomorphism kα NGe (e ◦ P ) ∼      = kα NGf (f ◦ Q) induces a k-algebra isomorphism
                              ∼
φ̄ : kα NGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) = kα NGf (f ◦ Q)/(f ◦ Q).

Notation 2.10. Let C be a finite category, R a finite subfield of k and α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ) ⊆

which sends a morphism (s, a) in Ĉ to the morphism s in C. The isomorphism class of the
extension Cˆ of C by R× depends only on the class of α in H 2 (C; R× ). It is clear that Cˆ is
finite. If C is an EI-category, then Cˆ is an EI-category as well.

Using the above two equalities, we obtain πf ◦ φ̂((x, λ)) = φ ◦ πe ((x, λ)), whence (ii).

3. Weights of kα OC and proof of Theorem 1.6
Definition 3.1 ([6, 1.4]). Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (C; k × ). A weight of kα C is a
pair (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e of an object X in C and a projective
simple kα Ge -module T .
   In the rest of this section, let C be a finite category with p-transporter category TC and
associated p-orbit category OC . The canonical functor TC → OC is the identity on objects,
and surjective on morphisms between any pair of objects in TC . For any object (X, P ) in TC ,
the kernel of the canonical moniod homomorphism EndTC ((X, P )) → EndOC ((X, P )) can be
identified with P . For any two objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q) in TC , the canonical map

                       HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) → HomOC ((X, P ), (Y, Q))

induces a bijection between the sets Q\HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) and HomOC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)).
Lemma 3.2 ([4, Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.4]). Let (X, P ) and (Y, Q) be objects in TC . Identify
morphisms between (X, P ) and (Y, Q) in TC (resp. OC ) with their canonical images in
HomC (X, Y ) (resp. Q\HomC (X, Y )/P ). Let e ∈ EndTC ((X, P )) and f ∈ EndTC ((Y, Q)) be
idempotent endomorphisms. Denote by ē = P ◦ e ◦ P = P ◦ e the canonical image of e in
EndOC ((X, P )), and by Ge the group of invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e.
The following hold:
  (i) For any idempotent d′ ∈ EndOC ((X, P )), there is an idempotent d ∈ EndTC ((X, P ))
      such that d′ = P ◦ d ◦ P .
 (ii) The idempotents e and f are isomorphic in TC if and only if ē and f¯ are isomorphic
      idempotents in OC .
(iii) The group of invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndTC ((X, P )) ◦ e is equal to NGe (e ◦
      P ).
(iv) The group of invertible elements in the monoid ē ◦ EndOC ((X, P )) ◦ ē is equal to NGe (e ◦
      P )/(e ◦ P ).
                                                12
Remark 3.3. By Lemma 3.2, we easily see that:
    (i) The isomorphism φ|kα NGe (e◦P ) : kα NGe (e ◦ P ) ∼    = kα NGf (f ◦ Q) in Proposition 2.9
coincides the isomorphism obtained by applying Proposition 2.2 (i) to TC , (e, P, P ), (f, Q, Q),
(s, P, Q), (t, Q, P ) instead of C, e, f , s, t, respectively.
    (ii) The isomorphism φ̄ : kα NGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) ∼   = kα NGf (f ◦ Q)/(f ◦ Q) in Proposition
2.9 coincides the isomorphism obtained by applying Proposition 2.2 (i) to OC , (e, P, P ),
(f, Q, Q), (s, P, Q), (t, Q, P ) instead of C, e, f , s, t, respectively. Here the overline notation
denotes taking the canonical image in OC .

Remark 3.4. Let α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; k × ).
    (i) Combining Definition 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, we see that: a weight of kα OC is exactly a
pair (ē, T ), where ē = P ◦ e ◦ P for some idempotent endomorphism e of some object X in
C, P is a not necessarily unitary p-subgroup of the moniod EndC (X), and T is a projective
simple kα NGe (e◦P )/(e◦P )-module. We identify the weight (ē, T ), the quadruple (e, P, P, T )
and the pair ((e, P, P ), T ). Note that (e, P, P ) is an idempotent endomorphism of (X, P ) in
the category TC . Consider Ge as a category with one object X, then (e◦P, T ) = (P ◦e◦P, T )
is a weight of kα OGe .
    (ii) Conversely, let X be an object in C and e ∈ EndC (X) an idempotent. A weight of
kα OGe is of the form (P, T ), where P is a p-subgroup of Ge , and T is a projective simple
kα NGe (P )/P -module. One easily sees that the pair (P, T ) = (P ◦ e ◦ P, T ) is also a weight
of kα OC .
    (iii) Let X and Y be objects in C. Let e ∈ EndC (X) and f ∈ EndC (Y ) be a pair of isomor-
phic idempotents. Let (P, T ) be a weight of kα OGe and (Q, T ′ ) a weight of kα OGf . Denote
by [(P, T )] ∈ W(kα OGe ) (resp. [(Q, T ′ )] ∈ W(kα OGf )) the isomorphism class of (P, T )
(resp. (Q, T ′ )). We say that [(P, T )] and [(Q, T ′ )] are isomorphic if the pairs ((e, P, P ), T )
and ((f, Q, Q), T ′ ) are isomorphic in the sense of Definition 2.3. In fact, this is equivalent
to that as weights of kα OC , (P, T ) and (Q, T ′ ) are in the same isomorphism class.
    (iv) Keep the notation in (iii) and assume that [(P, T )] and [(Q, T ′ )] are isomorphic.
Then by Proposition 2.8, there exist s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f
such that t ◦ s = e, s ◦ t = f and Q = s ◦ P ◦ t. Let φ be the k-algebra isomorphism
φ : kα Ge ∼ = kα Gf described in Proposition 2.2. By Proposition 2.9, φ induces a k-algebra
isomorphism φ̄ : kα NGe (P )/P ∼   = kα NGf (Q)/Q. The pairs ((e, P, P ), T ) and ((f, Q, Q), T ′ )
being isomorphic implies that the isomorphism classes of T and T ′ correspond to each other
via φ̄ (that is, T ′ ∼
                     = φ̄ T as kα NGf (Q)/Q-modules).
Lemma 3.5 ([4, Lemma 3.5]). Let E be a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes
of idempotent endomorphisms in C. For any e ∈ E, denote by Xe the object in C of which
e is an idempotent endomorphism, by Ge the subgroup of invertible elements of the monoid
e ◦ EndC (Xe ) ◦ e and by Xe a set of representatives of the Ge -conjugacy classes of p-subgroups
of Ge . Then the following hold:
  (i) The set {(Xe , P ) | e ∈ E, P ∈ Xe } is a set of representatives of the isomorphism
      classes of objects in TC .

                                                 13
 (ii) The set {(e, P, P ) | e ∈ E, P ∈ Xe } is a set of representatives of the isomorphism
      classes of idempotent endomorphisms in TC .
Combining (ii) and Lemma 3.2 (i), (ii) we also have:
     (iii) The set {(ē, P, P ) | e ∈ E, P ∈ Xe }, where ē = P ◦e◦P , is a set of representatives
           of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in OC .
Proposition 3.6. Let α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; k × ). Let X and Y be objects in C. Let e ∈ EndC (X) and
f ∈ EndC (Y ) be a pair of isomorphic idempotents.
  (i) For any weight (P, T ) of kα OGe , there is a unique isomorphism class [(Q, T ′ )] of weight
      of kα OGf isomorphic to [(P, T )].
                                                                                 ′
 (ii) Assume that α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; F× p ). The correspondence [(P, T )] 7→ [(Q, T )] defines a bi-
      jection Ωe,f : W(kα OGe ) → W(kα OGf ) which is commuting with the action of the
      Galois group Γ. In other words, for any σ ∈ Γ, [(P, T )] ∼     = [(Q, T ′ )] if and only if
      [(P, T )] ∼
           σ          σ  ′
                = [(Q, T )].
(iii) The inverse of the bijection Ωe,f is Ωf,e .
(iv) For any three isomorphic idempotents d, e and f in C, we have Ωe,f ◦ Ωd,e = Ωd,f .
Proof. By Lemma 3.5 (ii), up to Gf -conjugation there is a unique p-subgroup Q of Gf
such that (f, Q, Q) is isomorphic to (e, P, P ) in TC . By Proposition 2.8, there exist s ∈
f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f such that t ◦ s = e, s ◦ t = f and Q = s ◦ P ◦ t.
Let φ be the k-algebra isomorphism φ : kα Ge ∼       = kα Gf described in Proposition 2.2. By
Proposition 2.9, φ induces a k-algebra isomorphism φ̄ : kα NGe (P )/P ∼      = kα NGf (Q)/Q. Then
there is a unique isomorphism class of simple kα NGf (Q)-module, say [T ′ ], such that [T ]
and [T ′ ] correspond to each other via φ̄. Hence [(Q, T ′ )] is the unique isomorphism class of
weight of kα OGf isomorphic to [(P, T )], proving statement (i). For statement (ii), note that
     ∼ ′                σ        ∼σ ′                      2      ×
φ̄ T = T if and only if (φ̄ T ) = T . Since α is in Z (C; Fp ), by the explicit construction of
the isomorphism φ in Proposition 2.2 (i), φ̄ is defined over Fp . Using a similar argument as
in the proof of Proposition 2.5, we have σ (φ̄ T ) ∼
                                                   = φ̄ (σ T ) as kα NGf (Q)/Q-modules. Therefore,
     ∼ ′                    σ    ∼σ ′
φ̄ T = T if and only if φ̄ ( T ) = T , whence (ii). Statements (iii) and (iv) are trivial.

Proof of Theorem 1.6. We will use the notation of Lemma 3.5. By Theorem 2.4, there is a
bijection                                    G
                               Π : S(kα C) →    S(kα Ge ),
                                                     e∈E
                   F
where the symbol      denotes the disjoint union. By Proposition 2.6, Π is commuting with
the action of Γ. By assumption, the GAWC holds for kα Ge , that is, for any e ∈ E there is a
Γ-equivariant bijection                   G
                             S(kα Ge ) →      Z(kα NGe (P )/P ),
                                           P ∈Xe

where Z(kα NGe (P )/P ) is the set of isomorphism classes of projective simple kα NGe (P )/P -
modules. Hence there is a bijection
                                         G G
                             S(kα C) →          Z(kα NGe (P )/P )
                                         e∈E P ∈Xe
                                               14
commuting with the action of Γ. It remains to show that the right side corresponds to a
set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of weights of kα OC . In this double union,
e runs over E and P over Xe . By Lemma 3.5 (ii), this implies that the triples (e, P, P ) runs
over a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in
TC . By Lemma 3.2 (ii), the images of the triples in the morphism sets of OC runs over a
set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in OC . By
Lemma 3.2 (iv), the maximal subgroup determined by the image of any such (e, P, P ) in
OC is NGe (P )/P , and hence when [S] runs over Z(kα NGe (P )/P ), the quadruple (e, P, P, S)
runs over a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of weights of kα OC associated
with the image of (e, P, P ) in OC . Therefore, the double union corresponds to a set of
representatives the isomorphism classes of weights of kα OC .

4. The Brauer construction applied to twisted group algebras
    Let G be a finite group. A G-algebra over k is a k-algebra A endowed with an action
of G by k-algebra automorphisms, denoted a 7→ g a, where a ∈ A and g ∈ G. For any
p-subgroup P of G, we denote by AP the NG (P )-subalgebra of P -fixed points of A. For
any two p-subgroups Q ≤ P of G, the relative trace map TrPQ : AQ → AP is defined by
TrPQ (a) = x∈[P/Q] x a, where [P/Q] denotes a set of representatives of the left cosets of Q in
          P

P . We denote by A(P ) the P -Brauer quotient of A, i.e., the NG (P )-algebra
                                          X
                                     AP /    TrPQ (AQ ).
                                           Q<P


We denote by brA       P
                  P : A → A(P ) the canonical map, which is called the P -Brauer homomor-
phism. If f : A → B is a homomorphism of G-algebras, then f restricts to a homomorphism
of NG (P )-algebras f P : AP → B P , which in turn induces a homomorphism of NG (P )-
algebras f (P ) : A(P ) → B(P ) sending brA            B                       P
                                            P (a) to brP (f (a)) for any a ∈ A . In other
                          A      B    P
words, we have f (P ) ◦ brP = brP ◦ f . In this way, the P -Brauer construction defines a
functor (called the P -Brauer functor) from the category of G-algebras to the category of
NG (P )-algebras.
Lemma 4.1 (cf. e.g. [10, Exercise 11.4 or Proposition 27.6 (a)]). Let G be a finite group
and P a p-subgroup of G. Let A be a G-algebra over k. If A has a P -stable k-basis X, then
{brA            P                                P            u
   P (a) | a ∈ X } is a k-basis of A(P ), where X := {x ∈ X | x = x, ∀ u ∈ P }.

4.2. Let G be a finite group, P a p-subgroup of G and α ∈ Z 2 (G; k × ). Then both kG and
kα G are G-algebras via conjugation action of G. Since kG has an obvious P -stable k-basis
G, then by Lemma 4.1, we have (kG)(P ) ∼     = kCG (P ). But it is not very obvious that kα G
has a P -stable k-basis. To obtain (kα G)(P ) ∼ = kα CG (P ), we can not directly use Lemma
4.1. Since G is finite and since any finite subset of k = Fp is contained in a finite subfield of
k, we may assume that α ∈ Z 2 (G; R× ) for a finite subfield R of k. Let Ĝ be the extension of
G by R× associated with α; see Notation 2.10. Recall from Notation 2.10 and Proposition
2.11 that Ĝ has the following properties:
                                               15
  (i) Ĝ = {(g, r) | g ∈ G, r ∈ R× }. Denote by τ the canonical surjection Ĝ → G sending
      (g, r) to g for any g ∈ G and r ∈ R× . Then ker(τ ) = {(1, r) | r ∈ R× } ∼   = R× is a
      central subgroup of Ĝ of order not divisible by p.
 (ii) Write eR := |R1× | r∈R× r−1 (1, α(1, 1)−1 r). Then eR is an idempotent in Z(k Ĝ) and we
                        P

     have a k-algebra isomorphism π : k ĜeR → kα G sending (g, r) ∈ Ĝ to rg ∈ kα G.
Since P is a p-subgroup of G and since p ∤ | ker(τ )|, there is a p-subgroup P̂ of Ĝ such that
P̂ ∼
   = P via τ . Denote by û the preimage of u ∈ P in P̂ . Then P̂ = {û | u ∈ P }.
Proposition 4.3. Keep the notation of 4.2. For any t ∈ k Ĝ and g ∈ G, set g t =
(g, 1)t(g, 1)−1 ; clearly g t = (g, r)t(g, r)−1 for any r ∈ R× . This defines an action of G
on k Ĝ, and the isomorphism π : k ĜeR ∼   = kα G in 4.2 is an isomorphism of G-algebras.
Proof. This can be checked straightforward by definition.
Proposition 4.4. Keep the notation of 4.2. The following hold:
  (i) τ −1 (CG (P )) = CĜ (P̂ ) and τ −1 (NG (P )) = NĜ (P̂ ).
 (ii) The G-algebra isomorphism π : k ĜeR ∼          = kα G restricts to isomorphisms of NG (P )-
      algebras
                                           kCĜ (P̂ )eR ∼
                                                        = kα CG (P )
     and
                                       kNĜ (P̂ )eR ∼
                                                    = kα NG (P ),
      where the restrictions of α to subgroups of G are abusively again denoted by α.
(iii) The NG (P )-algebra isomorphism kNĜ (P̂ )eR ∼    = kα NG (P ) induces an NG (P )-algebra
      isomorphism
                                   kNĜ (P̂ )/P̂ ēR ∼
                                                     = kα NG (P )/P,
     where ēR is the canonical image of eR in NĜ (P̂ )/P̂ .
(iv) If α ∈ Z 2 (C; F×
                     p ), then all isomorphisms in (ii) and (iii) are defined over Fp .

Proof. Clearly we have CĜ (P̂ ) ⊆ τ −1 (CG (P )) and NĜ (P̂ ) ⊆ τ −1 (NG (P )). For any a ∈
τ −1 (CG (P )), since τ (a) ∈ CG (P ), we have aûa−1 û−1 ∈ ker(τ ) for all u ∈ P . It follows
that aûa−1 = ûz for some z ∈ ker(τ ). Since aûa−1 is a p-element of Ĝ, ûz should also be
a p-element of Ĝ. This forces z = 1 and hence a ∈ CĜ (P̂ ). Let a ∈ τ −1 (NG (P )). Since
τ (a) ∈ NG (P ), for any u ∈ P there exists v ∈ P such that τ (a)uτ (a)−1 = v. Equivalently,
we have τ (a)τ (û)τ (a−1 ) = τ (v̂). This implies that aûa−1 = v̂z for some z ∈ ker(τ ). Since
aûa−1 is a p-element of Ĝ, v̂z should also be a p-element of Ĝ. This again forces z = 1 and
hence a ∈ NĜ (P̂ ), completing the proof of (i). Statements (ii), (iii) and (iv) follows from (i)
and the explicit construction of π in 4.2 (iii).
   Let A be a finite-dimensional k-algebra. By a block of A, we mean a primitive central
idempotent of A. The k-algebra Ab = bAb is called a block algebra of A. For any indecom-
posable A-module U , there is a unique block b of A such that bU ̸= 0, and hence U is an
Ab-module.

                                                     17
Definition 4.6. Let G be a finite group, P a p-subgroup of G and α ∈ Z 2 (G; k × ). Let b
be a central idempotent of kα G, c a block of kα NG (P ) and U an indecomposable kα NG (P )-
module. We say that c (resp. U ) is associated to b if brkPα G (b)c ̸= 0 (resp. brkPα G (b)U ̸= 0).
By Proposition 4.5 (iv), there is a unique block of kα G to which c (resp. U ) is associated.
Assume that α ∈ Z 2 (G; F× p ). Let σ be an element of Γ = Gal(k/Fp ). In this case the Brauer
                                                           (F ) G
map brP is defined over Fp (because brkPα G = Idk ⊗ brP p α ), hence commuting with σ.

Since σ commutes with the Brauer map brP , we see that σ(c) (resp. σ U ) is associated
to σ(b) if and only if c (resp. U ) is associated to b. Hence the group Γb acts on the set of
isomorphism classes of indecomposable kα NG (P )-modules associated to b.

5. EI-categories C and partition of weights of kα OC by blocks of kα C
   The following proposition is the reason why we can give a partition of weights of kα OC
by blocks of kα C for an EI-category C.
Proposition 5.1. Let R be a commutative ring, C a finite category, α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ) and b a
central idempotent of Rα C. Let e be an idempotent endomorphism of an object X in C and
let ê = α(e, e)−1 e. Then êb is a central idempotent in the subalgebra Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e) of
Rα C. In particular, if C is an EI-category, then e = IdX and êb is a central idempotent of
Rα Ge .
Proof. Since ê is the unit element of Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e), it suffices to show that êb is
contained in the subalgebra Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e). Since ê is an idempotent in Rα C and since
b ∈ Z(Rα C), we have êb = ê2 b = êbê. Since ê is an R-linear combination of elements of
e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e, by the definition of the multiplication in Rα C, we see that êbê is an R-linear
combination of elements of e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e. Hence êb ∈ Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e), proving the
first statement. If C is an EI-category, then IdX is the unique idempotent in EndC (X) and
we have e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e = GIdX . This completes the proof.
Proposition 5.2. Let C a finite EI-category, α ∈ Z 2 (C; k × ) and b a central idempotent
of kα C. Let X and Y be objects in C. Set e = IdX , f = IdY , ê = α(e, e)−1 e and fˆ =
α(f, f )−1 f . Assume that e is isomorphic to f . Then there exist s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and
t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t ◦ s = e and s ◦ t = f . Let φ be the k-algebra isomorphism
kα Ge ∼
      = kα Gf described in Proposition 2.2 (i). Then φ(êb) = fˆb.
Proof. Since C is finite and since any finite subset of k = Fp is contained in a finite subfield
of k, we may assume that α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ) for a finite subfield R of k. By the commutative
diagram in Proposition 2.13 (ii), we may assume that α is trivial. Then φ is the k-algebra
isomorphism kGe ∼  = kGf sending x ∈ kGe to sxt. Since b is in the center of kC, we have
φ(eb) = sebt = setb = f b, whence the result.
Proposition 5.3 (a generalisation of Proposition 5.2). Let C be a finite EI-category, α ∈
Z 2 (OC ; k × ) and b a central idempotent of kα C. Let X and Y be objects in C. Set e = IdX ,
f = IdY , ê = α(e, e)−1 e and fˆ = α(f, f )−1 f . Assume that e is isomorphic to f . Then there
exist s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t ◦ s = e and s ◦ t = f .

φ restricts to a k-algebra isomorphism kα NGe (P ) ∼

Definition 5.4. Keep the notation of Remark 3.4 (i). Assume further that C is an EI-
category. Then e = IdX . Set ê = α(e, e)−1 e. We regard T as a simple kα NGe (P )-module
via the canonical surjection kα NGe (P ) → kα NGe (P )/P . Let b be a central idempotent of
kα C. Then by Proposition 5.1, êb is in kα Ge . We say that (ē, T ) is a b-weight of kα OC
if T is associated to the central idempotent êb of kα Ge ; by Definition 4.6 this means that
brkPα Ge (êb)T ̸= 0. If the pair (f¯, T ′ ) is another weight of kα OC isomorphic to (ē, T ), then by
Proposition 5.3 we see that (ē, T ) is a b-weight if and only if (f¯, T ′ ) is a b-weight. Hence b also
gives a partition of isomorphism classes of weights of kα OC . We denote by W(kα OC , b) the
set of isomorphism classes of b-weights; clearly we have W(kα OC , 1) = W(kα OC ). Let σ ∈ Γ.
Assume that (ē, T ) is a b-weight of kα OC , or equivalently, T is associated to the central
idempotent êb of kα Ge . Then by Definition 4.6, σ T is associated to the central idempotent
σ(êb) = êσ(b) of kα Ge . This implies that (ē, σ T ) is a σ(b)-weight of kα OC . Hence the action
of Γ on the set of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kα OC restricts to an action of Γb on
the set of (isomorphism classes of) b-weights of kα OC .
Remark 5.5. Definition 5.4 gives a partition of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kα OC
by a central idempotent (and hence a block) of kα C for any finite EI-category C. If C is
not EI, then we don’t know whether êb lies in kα Ge , hence we can no longer have such a
partition.
Theorem 5.6 (a block-theoretic refinement of Theorem 2.4). Let R be a commutative ring,
C a finite EI-category, α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ) and b a central idempotent of kα C. The map sending
a simple Rα Cb-module S to the pair (e, eS), where e is an idempotent endomorphism in
C minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0, induces a bijection Πb between S(Rα Cb) and the set of
isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a
simple Rα Ge (bê)-module T , where ê = α(e, e)−1 e.
                                                               20
Proof. Let e be an idempotent endomorphism in C. Since C is EI, e = IdX for some object
X in C. By Proposition 5.1, êb is a central idempotent in Rα Ge = Rα Ge ê. If S is a simple
Rα Cb-module, then eS is an Rα Ge (êb)-module. Since eS is also a simple Rα Ge -module (see
Theorem 2.4), it is a simple Rα Ge (êb)-module. Hence the map Π in Theorem 2.4 restricts
to a map Πb from S(Rα Cb) to the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an
idempotent endomorphism e in C and a simple Rα Ge (bê)-module T . Since
                                                G
                           S(Rα C) = S(Rα Cb) S(Rα C(1 − b))

and                                                          G
                 S(Rα Ge ) = S(Rα Ge ê) = S(Rα Ge (êb))        S(Rα Ge (ê(1 − b))),
the union of the maps Πb and Π1−b is exactly the bijection Π in Theorem 2.4. Hence Πb is
a bijection.

    It remains to show that the right side corresponds to a set of representatives of the

By Lemma 3.5 (ii), this implies that the triples (e, P, P ) runs over a set of representatives
of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in TC . By Lemma 3.2 (ii), the
images of the triples in the morphism sets of OC runs over a set of representatives of the
isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in OC . By Lemma 3.2 (iv), the maximal
subgroup determined by the image of any such (e, P, P ) in OC is NGe (P )/P , and hence
when [S] runs over Z(kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb))), the quadruple (e, P, P, S) runs over a set
of representatives of the isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC associated with the image
of (e, P, P ) in OC . Therefore, the double union corresponds to a set of representatives the
isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC .

Remark 5.9. In Theorem 1.14, the assumption that α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; F×        p ) is only using for
ensuring that we can consider the actions of Γb . If we consider the non-Galois version of the
blockwise Alperin weight conjecture (BAWC), then we can assume that α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; k × ).
The proof of Theorem 1.14 can be easily adapted to a proof of the statement that: if for
any idempotent endomorphism e in C, there is a bijection S(kα Ge êb) → W(kα OGe , êb), then
there exists a bijection S(kα Cb) → W(kα OC , b). In particular, the BAWC for finite twisted
EI-categorie algebras and finite twisted group algebras are equivalent.

    For the proof of Theorem 1.14, we have developed many auxiliary results. Using part
of those auxiliary results, we show the BGAWC for finite twisted EI-category algebras and
finite ordinary EI-category algebras are equivalent:

bijection S(kα Cπ(b)) → W(kα OC , π(b)). In particular, the BAWC for finite twisted EI-
category algebras and finite ordinary EI-category algebras are equivalent.

6. Automorphisms of categories and proof of Theorem 1.20
   Let C be a finite category and F ∈ Aut(C). For any object X in C, F defines an
isomorphism FX : EndC (X) → EndC (F(X)) of moniods; for shorthand we abusively denote
the isomorphism FX by F. Let e be an idempotent in EndC (X). Then F(e) is an idempotent
in EndC (F(X)). The monoid isomorphism F : EndC (X) → EndC (F(X)) restricts to a
group isomorphism Fe : Ge → GF (e) , which in turn extends to a k-algebra isomorphism
kGe → kGF (e) still denoted by Fe . For any kGe -module U , we set F U to be the kGF (e) -
module Fe U and set F [U ] to be [F U ].
Proposition 6.1. Let C be a finite category and F ∈ Aut(C). There is a well-defined action
of the automorphism group Aut(C) on the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting
of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a simple kGe -module T via F (e, T ) = (F(e), Fe T ).
Sometimes we will also write F (P, T ) as F (P, T ). Moreover, (e, T ) is a weight if and only if
(F(e), Fe T ) is a weight.
Proof. By the definition of being isomorphic (see the first paragraph of Section 2), it is
clear that two idempotent endomorphisms e and e′ are isomorphic if and only if F(e) and
F(e′ ) are isomorphic. For the first statement we need to show that if (e, T ) is isomorphic to
(e′ , T ′ ), then (F(e), Fe T ) is isomorphic to (F(e′ ), Fe′ (T ′ )). By Proposition 2.2 (i), there is a
k-algebra isomorphism φ : kGe → kGe′ . The group isomorphisms Fe : Ge → GF (e) and Fe′ :
Ge′ → GF (e′ ) induce k-algebra isomorphisms Fe : kGe → kGF (e) and Fe′ : kGe′ → kGF (e′ ) ,
respectively. Let Fφ := Fe′ ◦ φ ◦ Fe−1 . We need to show that the isomorphism classes of Fe T
and Fe′ T ′ correspond to each other through the induced isomorphism Fφ : kGF (e) → kGF (e′ ) .
                                                   23
In other words, we need to show that Fφ (Fe T ) ∼   = Fe′ T ′ as kGF (e′ ) -modules. Since (e, T ) is
isomorphic to (e′ , T ′ ), there is an isomorphism φ T ∼
                                                       = T ′ of kGe′ -modules. It follows that
                                                                       ∼      ′
                         Fφ (Fe T ) = Fφ ◦Fe T = Fe′ ◦φ T = Fe′ (φ T ) = Fe′ T ,


as required. This proves the first statement. For the second statement, we need to show that
T is a projective kGe -module if and only if Fe T is a projective kGF (e) -module. It suffices
to show that Fe kGe ∼  = kGF (e) as kGF (e) -modules. Indeed, the map sending a ∈ Fe kGe to
Fe (a) ∈ kGF (e) is a desired isomorphism.

Proposition 6.2. Keep the notation of Theorem 2.4. Assume that R = k and α is trivial.
Then the bijection Π commutes with the action of the automorphism group Aut(C).

Proof. Let F ∈ Aut(C) and S a simple kC-module. Denote by [S] the isomorphism class of S.
Let e be an idempotent endomorphism in C, minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0. Then one easily
checks that F S is a simple kC-module, F(e)(F S) is a kGF (e) -module, and F(e)(F S) ∼
                                                                                     = F (eS)
as kGF (e) -modules. Hence by the minimality of e, we see that F(e) is minimal with respect
to F(e)(F S) ̸= 0. Therefore, we have

          Π([F S]) = [(F(e), F(e)(F S))] = [(F(e), F (eS))] = F [(e, eS)] = F (Π([S])),

where the notation [(e, S)] denotes the isomorphism class of (e, S), and where the third
equality holds by Proposition 6.1.

Proposition 6.3. Keep the notation of Theorem 5.6. Let H be any subgroup of Γ. Assume
that R = k and α is trivial. Then the bijection Πb commutes with the action of the group
(H × Aut(C))b .

Proof. Since Πb is a part of the bijection Π in Theorem 2.4, the statement follows from
Propositions 2.6 and 6.2.
                                                                                       kG

(kG) → kCG (P ) the map sending g∈G αg g (where αg ∈ k) to g∈CG (P ) αg g. Let b be a
central idempotent of kG, c a block of kNG (P ) and U an indecomposable kNG (P )-module.
By Definition 4.6, c (resp. U ) is associated to b if brkG                   kG

By Proposition 4.5 (iv), there is a unique block of kG to which c (resp. U ) is associated.
Let G′ be another finite group and F : G ∼  = G′ a group isomorphism. Then F extends
k-linearly to a k-algebra isomorphism kG ∼ = kG′ which in turn restricts to k-algebra iso-
morphisms kCG (P ) ∼ = kCG′ (F(P )) and kNG (P ) ∼

Therefore, F(c) (resp. F U ) is associated to F(b) if and only if c (resp. U ) is associated

kNG (P )-modules associated to b. The isomoprhism F : NG (P ) ∼            = NG′ (F(P )) induces a
                                       ∼
k-algebra isomorphism NG (P )/P = NG′ (F(P ))/F(P ) still denoted by F. For any weight
(P, T ) of kOG , we set F (P, T ) to be (F(P ), F T ), which is a weight of kOG′ . One easily checks
that if (P, T ) and (Q, T ′ ) are isomorphic weights of kOG , then (F(P ), F T ) and (F(Q), F T ′ )
are isomorphic weights of kOG′ ; we set F [(P, T )] := [F (P, T )].
6.5. (i) Let C be a finite category and F ∈ Aut(C). Then F induces an automorphism TF
of TC sending an object (X, P ) in TC to (F(X), F(P )) ∈ TC with the obvious maps induced
by F on morphism sets. Similarly, F induces an automorphism OF of OC sending an object
(X, P ) in OC to (F(X), F(P )) ∈ OC . By Proposition 6.1, the automorphism OF acts on
the set of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kOC . Hence we can define an action of Aut(C)
on the set of (isomorphism classes of) weights of kOC by letting F act as OF . With the
notation of Remark 3.4 (i), we see that a weight of kOC is a pair (ē, T ), where ē = P ◦ e ◦ P
for some idempotent endomorphism e of some object X in C, P is a not necessarily unitary
p-subgroup of the moniod EndC (X), and T is a projective simple kNGe (e◦P )/(e◦P )-module.
The automorphism F of C induces a group isomorphism

                  NGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) ∼
                                        = NGF (e) (F(e) ◦ F(P ))/(F(e) ◦ F(P ))

which in turn induces a k-algebra isomorphism

                kNGe (e ◦ P )/(e ◦ P ) ∼
                                       = kNGF (e) (F(e) ◦ F(P ))/(F(e) ◦ F(P ));

we again abusively denote these isomorphisms by F. Write F(ē) := F(P ) ◦ F(e) ◦ F(P ).
Then by definition, we have
                                 F
                                     (ē, T ) = OF (ē, T ) = (F(ē), F T ).

    (ii) Assume further that C is a finite EI-category and b is a central idempotent in kC.
Assume that (ē, T ) is a b-weight of kOC , or equivalently, T is associated to the central
idempotent eb of kGe . Then by Remark 6.4, F T is associated to the central idempotent
F(eb) = F(e)F(b) of kGF (e) . This implies that (F(ē), F T ) is an F(b)-weight of kOC . Let H
be any subgroup of Γ. Then the action of H × Aut(C) on the set of (isomorphism classes of)
weights of kOC restricts to an action of (H × Aut(C))b on the set of (isomorphism classes
of) b-weights of kOC .
Proposition 6.6. Let C be a finite category (resp. EI-category) and b the unit element (resp.
a central idempotent) of kC. Then for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, eb is a central
idempotent in kGe ; see Proposition 5.1 below. Let H be any subgroup of Γ. Assume that
for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, there is a bijection Ωe : S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb)
fulfilling the following conditions:
  (i) For any idempotent e in C and any simple kGe eb-module T , ΩF (e) ((σ,F ) [T ]) = (σ,F ) Ωe ([T ])
      for any (σ, F) ∈ (H × Aut(C))b .
                                                      25
 (ii) For any isomorphic idempotents e and f in C, we have Ωf ◦ Λe,f = Ωe,f ◦ Ωe , where
      Λf,e is defined as in Notation 2.7 and Ωe,f is defined as in Proposition 3.6.
    Then there exists an (H × Aut(C))b -equivariant bijection S(kCb) → W(kOC , b).

Proof. We will use the notation of Lemma 3.5. By Theorem 5.6, there is a bijection

Proposition 6.7. Let C be a finite category (resp. EI-category) and b the unit element
(resp. a central idempotent) of kC. Then for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, eb is a
central idempotent in kGe ; see Proposition 5.1. Let H be any subgroup of Γb . Assume that
for any idempotent endomorphism e in C there is an (H × Aut(Ge ))be -equivariant bijection
Ω′e : S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb). Then we can modify the choices of some bijections and
obtain a family of (H × Aut(Ge ))be -equivariant bijections {Ωe : S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb)}
satisfying the following two conditions in Proposition 6.6:
  (i) For any idempotent e in C and any simple kGe eb-module T , ΩF (e) ((σ,F ) [T ]) = (σ,F ) Ωe ([T ])
      for any (σ, F) ∈ (H × Aut(C))b .
 (ii) For any objects X, Y in C and any isomorphic idempotents e ∈ EndC (X), f ∈ EndC (Y ),
      we have Ωf ◦Λe,f = Ωe,f ◦Ωe , where Λf,e is defined as in Notation 2.7 and Ωe,f is defined
      as in Proposition 3.6.

Proof. Let I be the set of all idempotent endomorphisms in C. Define a relation on the
set I by e ∼ f , if there exists a group isomorphism ψ : Ge ∼   = Gf such that the induced
k-algebra isomorphism ψ : kGe ∼   = kGf satisfying ψ(eb) = f σ −1 (b) for some σ ∈ H. For
convenience, we say that the pair (σ, ψ) belongs to (H × Iso(Ge , Gf ))b . One easily checks
that the relation ∼ is an equivalence relation. By Proposition 5.2, if e and f are isomorphic
idempotent endomorphisms in C, then e ∼ f . Also, if e and f are idempotent endomorphisms
in C such that f = F(e) for some (σ, F) ∈ (H × Aut(C))b , then e ∼ f . Let I0 ⊆ I be a
set of representatives of the equivalence classes of the relation ∼. For any e ∈ I0 , we set
                                                           27
Ωe := Ω′e . Let f be an arbitrary idempotent endomorphism in C. There exists a unique
idempotent e ∈ I0 such that e ∼ f . By definition, there is a group isomorphism ψ : Ge ∼           = Gf
with the induced k-algebra isomorphism ψ : kGe ∼         =  kG f satisfying ψ(eb) = f σ −1
                                                                                           (b) for some
σ ∈ H. By Remark 6.4, if (P, T ) is a weight of kOGe , then (ψ(P ), ψ T ) is a weight of kOGf .
Now we see that if (P, T ) is an eb-weight of kOGe , then (ψ(P ), σ (ψ T )) is an f b-weight of
kOGf . For any simple kGf f b-module T , we define Ωf ([T ]) to be (σ,ψ) Ωe ((σ−1 ,ψ−1 ) [T ]) :=
σ               −1
  (ψ Ωe (ψ−1 [σ T ])). Since Ωe is (H × Aut(Ge ))b -equivariant, Ωf is independent of the choice
of the pair (σ, ψ). One easily checks that Ωf is a bijection from S(kGf f b) to W(kOGf , f b).
We claim that Ωf is (H × Aut(Gf ))f b -equivariant. Let (σ ′ , F) ∈ (H × Aut(Gf ))f b . Then
(σ −1 , ψ −1 ) ◦ (σ ′ , F) ◦ (σ, ψ) ∈ (H × Aut(Ge ))eb . For any simple kGf f b-module T , we have

       Ωf ((σ′ ,F ) [T ]) = (σ,ψ) Ωe ((σ−1 ,ψ−1 )◦(σ′ ,F ) T ) = (σ,ψ) Ωe ((σ−1 ,ψ−1 )◦(σ′ ,F )◦(σ,ψ)◦(σ−1 ,ψ−1 ) T )
                          = (σ,ψ)◦(σ−1 ,ψ−1 )◦(σ′ ,F )◦(σ,ψ) Ωe ((σ−1 ,ψ−1 ) T ) = (σ′ ,F )◦(σ,ψ) Ωe ((σ−1 ,ψ−1 ) T )
                          = (σ′ ,F ) Ωf ([T ]),

as claimed. Next we show that the family of bijections {Ωe : S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb)}
satisfies the required two conditions:
    Condition (i). Now let e be an arbitrary idempotent endomorphism in C. Let e0 be
the unique element in I0 such that e ∼ e0 via some pair (σ0 , ψ0 ) ∈ (H × Iso(Ge0 , Ge ))b . Let
(σ, F) be an arbitrary element of (H × Aut(C))b . Write σ ′ = σ ◦ σ0 and ψ ′ = F ◦ ψ0 . Then
we have (σ ′ , ψ ′ ) ∈ (H × Iso(Ge0 , GF (e) ))b . For any simple kGe eb-module T ,

               ΩF (e) ((σ,F ) [T ]) = (σ′ ,ψ′ ) Ωe0 ((σ′ −1 ,ψ′ −1 )◦(σ,F ) T ) = (σ′ ,ψ′ ) Ωe0 ((σ0−1 ,ψ0−1 ) T )
                                     = (σ′ ,ψ′ )◦(σ0−1 ,ψ0−1 )◦(σ0 ,ψ0 ) Ωe0 ((σ0−1 ,ψ0−1 ) T )
                                     = (σ,F ) Ωe ([T ])

where the first and fourth equalities hold by the definitions of ΩF (e) and Ωe , respectively.
Therefore, the family of bijections {Ωe : S(kGe eb) → W(kOGe , eb)} satisfies condition (i).
    Condition (ii). Let us first assume that e ∈ I0 . Let s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and
t ∈ e◦HomC (Y, X)◦f satisfying t◦s = e and s◦t = f . Then we have a group isomorphism φ :
Ge ∼
   = Gf sending x ∈ Ge to s◦x◦t. By Proposition 5.2, we have (Idk , φ) ∈ (H ×Iso(Ge , Gf ))b .
For any simple kGf f b-module T , by definition of Ωf , we have

                Ωf ([T ]) = (Idk ,φ) Ωe ((Idk ,φ−1 ) T ) = φ Ωe (φ−1 T ) = Ωe,f ◦ Ωe ◦ Λf,e ([T ])

where the third equality holds by the definitions of Λf,e and Ωe,f . Now let us remove the
assumption that e ∈ I0 . Since e and f are isomorphic idempotents, there is a unique
idempotent d ∈ I0 such that e ∼ d ∼ f . Then by the argument above, we have Ωe :=
Ωd,e ◦ Ωd ◦ Λe,d and Ωf := Ωd,f ◦ Ωd ◦ Λf,d . It follows that

                         Ωf = Ωd,f ◦ Ωe,d ◦ Ωe ◦ Λd,e ◦ Λf,d = Ωe,f ◦ Ωe ◦ Λf,e .

Equivalently, Ωf ◦ Λe,f = Ωe,f ◦ Ωe . Therefore, condition (ii) holds.
                                                               28
Proof of Theorem 1.20. This follows from Propositions 6.6 and 6.7.
